--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.label_propagation()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Semi-supervised label propagation for node classification. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.label_propagation()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Semi-supervised label propagation for node classification. title: >- [Graph.label_propagation()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Semi-supervised label propagation for node classification. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Semi-supervised label propagation for node classification. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L47517-L47689){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.label_propagation( known_labels, max_iter=100, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Label propagation](../assets/graphs/label-propagation.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two dense clusters, a triangle A, B, C and a four-node cluster D, E, F, G, joined by the edge C to D. Only A (id 1) and G (id 7) are given labels, 0 and 1, shown as badges; every other node adopts the label most common among its neighbors, so the triangle ends with label 0 (accent) and D, E, F, G with label 1 (teal)." width="100%"} Spreads known labels through the network: at each iteration every unlabeled node adopts the most common label among its neighbors (weighted by edge weight). Nodes whose labels are provided in `known_labels=` are held fixed throughout. This method needs some labels to start from. To find communities with no labels at all (what NetworkX calls `asyn_lpa_communities()`), use `cmty_label_propagation()`. This is a classic way to classify nodes when only a few of them have known classes: the assumption is that connected nodes tend to share a class (homophily), so labels "flow" from the seeds outward along edges. Typical uses include: - inferring the function of unannotated genes or proteins from annotated interaction partners - spreading a few known spam, fraud, or bot accounts through a social or transaction network - assigning nodes to known groups (e.g., two factions) from a handful of examples Nodes are updated one at a time, and each update immediately influences nodes visited later in the same iteration. Iteration stops early as soon as a full pass changes no label. Votes from neighbors are weighted by the edge `weight` (edges without a weight count as `1.0`). In directed graphs, both incoming and outgoing neighbors vote, so direction is effectively ignored. When two labels receive exactly equal votes, which one wins is arbitrary, so on symmetric graphs (such as a path with a seed at each end) the nodes in the middle may go either way. Unlike community detection with `cmty_louvain()` and friends, this method does not invent groups: every node ends up with one of the seed labels, or `-1` if no seed can reach it. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [known_labels]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict[Union[int, str], int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A `{node: class}` dictionary of seed labels. Keys are node IDs or string labels, and values are integers identifying the class. At least one entry is required, and every key must be a node in the graph. Avoid `-1` as a class value since it is used to mark unlabeled nodes. [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of propagation iterations (full passes over all nodes). Default is `100`. Propagation usually stops sooner, as soon as a pass changes nothing. In each pass a label can travel many hops, but in large or long, thin graphs a small value may stop propagation before labels have reached every node. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute (node DataFrame column) to store assignments in. If `None` (default), uses `"label_propagation"`. Overwrites the column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return a `{node_id: label}` dictionary directly. If `False` (default), store the result as a node attribute and return `self` for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: label assignments for every node, sorted by node ID. Seed nodes keep their given labels; nodes that could not be reached from any seed retain label `-1`. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): `self` for chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `known_labels=` is empty or contains a node ID not present in the graph. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~cmty_label_propagation`) : Find communities by label propagation, with no seed labels. [](`~network_smooth`) : Spread numeric scores over the network instead of classes. [](`~random_walk_with_restart`) : Score nodes by their closeness to a set of seeds. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A triangle and a four-node clique are joined by the edge `C`–`D`. Seeding `A` with class `0` and `G` with class `1` is enough to classify every node by the group it belongs to: ::: {#c4776349 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("D", "F"), ("D", "G"), ("E", "F"), ("E", "G"), ("F", "G")] ) ( graph.label_propagation({"A": 0, "G": 1}) .get_node_df() .select("label", "label_propagation") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
shape: (7, 2)
labellabel_propagation
stri64
"A"0
"B"0
"C"0
"D"1
"E"1
"F"1
"G"1
``` ::: ::: Edge weights decide close votes. `Xena` is tied to `Alice` (class `0`) by a weight of `3` and to `Bob` (class `1`) by a weight of `1`, so she takes Alice's class. `Zed`, with no path to a seed, keeps `-1`: ::: {#0d4d8d84 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph.from_edges([("Xena", "Alice", 3.0), ("Xena", "Bob", 1.0)]) graph.add_node(label="Zed") ( graph.label_propagation({"Alice": 0, "Bob": 1}) .get_node_df() .select("label", "label_propagation") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
shape: (4, 2)
labellabel_propagation
stri64
"Xena"0
"Alice"0
"Bob"1
"Zed"-1
``` ::: ::: ### Predicting what a protein does `proteins()` is a small protein interaction network. Every protein but three has a known pathway; ORF1, ORF2 and ORF3 are uncharacterized. Since proteins that bind tend to work together, the known pathways, numbered as classes, can be spread to the unknown ones: ::: {#73a97b82 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl proteins = ec.proteins() pathway = proteins.get_node_attrs("pathway") names = sorted(set(pathway.values())) classes = proteins.label_propagation( {node: names.index(p) for node, p in pathway.items()}, return_dict=True ) proteins.set_node_attrs( "predicted", {node: names[c] for node, c in classes.items()} ) ( proteins.get_node_df() .filter(pl.col("pathway").is_null()) .select("label", "predicted") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 2)
labelpredicted
strstr
"ORF1""DNA repair"
"ORF2""Signaling"
"ORF3""Transport"
``` ::: ::: Each takes the pathway of most of its partners: ORF1 sits among the DNA repair proteins, ORF2 among the signaling ones and ORF3 among the transport ones. Drawn by pathway before and after, the three gray proteins take their neighbors' colors: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#48c23db3 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} proteins.plot( layout="pos", color_by="pathway", label_by="label", legend=False, width=360, height=360, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
